title: Knee Replacement Risks: How Safe Is the Operation?
metaDescription: Is knee replacement safe? The real risks (clots, infection, stiffness), how common they are, how long a knee lasts, and who should think twice.
intro: Knee replacement is a well-established operation and most people have no complications. But it is still a major operation, and you should know the risks before deciding. The main ones are blood clots, wound infection and a knee that stays stiff or sore. Your age and general health affect your risk.

sections.heading: Is knee replacement a safe operation?
sections.body: Yes for most people. The NHS says most people who have a knee replacement have no complications, and the operation is usually very successful at reducing pain and improving movement. Safety depends on your age and general health, which we check carefully beforehand.

sections.heading: What are the main risks?
sections.body: The NHS lists these. Most can be treated, but it is right to know them.
bullets: Blood clots in the leg (DVT), which are often not serious but can sometimes travel to the lungs.
Wound infection, a small chance; usually treated with antibiotics, but a deep infection may need more surgery.
Damage to nerves, blood vessels or ligaments, which is uncommon.
Ongoing problems such as stiffness, lasting pain, or the knee feeling unstable.

sections.heading: How do you lower the risks?
sections.body: We check your heart, blood sugar, blood pressure and medicines before surgery, and you are encouraged to stop smoking. After surgery, early walking, leg exercises and compression stockings (usually for at least 6 weeks) lower the chance of clots. Good wound care and attending follow-up matter too.

sections.heading: Will it relieve all my pain?
sections.body: Not guaranteed. The NHS says surgery may greatly improve symptoms but cannot promise complete relief. Most people are much better; some still have some ache or stiffness. Physiotherapy after surgery is a big part of the result.

sections.heading: How long does a knee replacement last?
sections.body: The NHS says a knee replacement typically lasts about 25 years. Needing another operation later is not common, but possible, particularly for people who have surgery young.

sections.heading: Who should think twice?
sections.body: Anyone whose pain is still manageable with other treatment, or who is not ready for the recovery. Surgery should be your choice, not something you feel pushed into. If your health is a concern, we discuss that openly and may suggest first improving it.

faqs.q: What is the chance of complications after knee replacement?
faqs.a: Most people have none. The NHS gives no exact percentages, and risk depends on age and health.

faqs.q: How long is the hospital stay?
faqs.a: Most people go home 1 to 4 days after surgery.

faqs.q: When can I drive after knee replacement?
faqs.a: The NHS advises waiting at least 6 weeks after a total replacement, and 3 weeks after a partial one, after checking with your doctor.
Rarely, it can loosen, wear or become infected. Regular follow-up helps spot problems early.
Robotic assistance improves how accurately the implant is placed; surgeon experience still matters most.

faqs.q: Can I have both knees done together?
faqs.a: In suitable patients it is possible, but it carries more risk and needs careful assessment.
